summary: Describes the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP), an XML-based client-server protocol for provisioning objects in a shared central repository, such as domain registries. It defines generic operations and a framework for mapping them to object types. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Registries need a standard way for registrars to add and change domain names. EPP is the common language for that, like a form every registrar fills out the same way.

questions: how do registrars talk to domain registries
how does epp transfer a domain
subtitle: The XML protocol registrars use to create, change, renew and transfer objects such as domain names in a shared registry.

tldr.problem: Domain name registrars and registries needed a standard, extensible way for many service providers to manage objects in one shared central repository.
tldr.mechanism: EPP is a stateful XML protocol with a small set of atomic commands (login, check, info, poll, create, delete, renew, transfer, update). Object-specific details live in separate mappings, and results are four-digit codes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5730 is an Internet Standard (STD 69) that obsoletes RFC 4930. It leaves transport and strong security to lower layers, and mappings such as the domain mapping in RFC 5731 add the object details.

today: RFC 5730 is an Internet Standard (STD 69) and has not been obsoleted. It obsoletes RFC 4930, and object details such as domain names are defined in separate mappings like RFC 5731.

sections.title: What EPP Is For
sections.content:
The Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) version 1.0 is an XML text protocol that lets multiple service providers perform object-provisioning operations using a shared central object repository. It is specified with XML 1.0 and XML Schema, and its content is identified by the media type application/epp+xml.

The original motivation was a standard Internet domain name registration protocol between domain name registrars and domain name registries. The RFC expects additional uses beyond domain names. A client that is authorized to manage an existing object is called the sponsoring client.

EPP is meant for very different operating environments, so it is layered. Bindings to specific transport and security protocols are outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Many shops need to write names into one big shared notebook. EPP is the rulebook they all follow so the notebook stays neat and nobody gets confused.

sections.title: Sessions, Commands and Responses
sections.content:
EPP is stateful. After lower-layer security is in place, client and server exchange identification, authentication and option information, and then the client sends commands and the server answers each one. A server MUST answer a connection or <hello> with a <greeting>, and it MUST promptly answer each command.

All commands are atomic: there is no partial success or partial failure. They are also designed so that they can be made idempotent, so running a command twice has the same net effect as running it once. That makes retrying after a lost response safe, and success or failure MUST NOT be assumed if no response, or a malformed one, arrives.

Commands fall into three groups: session management (<login>, <logout>), queries (<check>, <info>, <poll>, <transfer> with op="query") and object transforms (<create>, <delete>, <renew>, <transfer>, <update>). Commands are processed in the order received.

A server may review a transform command offline. Then the response MUST say the command was processed but the action is pending, the object's state MUST show the pending action, and the server MUST notify the client when it finishes.
sections.plainLanguage: You knock, the server says hello, you show your ID, and then you ask for things one at a time. Each answer is either all done or not done at all, so asking twice never makes a mess.

sections.title: Greeting, Command and Response Formats
sections.content:
Every EPP XML instance starts with an <epp> element in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:epp-1.0. A <greeting> carries the server name (<svID>), its date and time in UTC (<svDate>), and a service menu listing supported protocol versions, response languages, object namespaces and optional extensions. It also carries a <dcp> data collection policy that must disclose what data is collected, for what purpose, who receives it and how long it is kept.

A command holds one command element, an optional <extension> and an optional client transaction identifier <clTRID>. A response holds one or more <result> elements, each with a four-digit code and a human-readable <msg> (English by default), plus optional <msgQ>, <resData> and <extension>, and a required <trID>.

The transaction identifier combines the client's <clTRID> and a server-assigned <svTRID>. Both sides SHOULD log, retain and protect these so their records stay consistent.

All date-time values MUST be in UTC, using the extended form with upper case T and Z. UTF-8 is the RECOMMENDED character encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message goes in the same kind of envelope. The server's hello says what it can do, and every answer has a ticket number so both sides can match questions with answers.

sections.title: The Extension Framework
sections.content:
EPP deliberately defines no objects of its own. It provides an extension framework at three levels: protocol extensions, object extensions and command-response extensions. Object-specific data sits in elements identified by XML namespaces, each pointing to a schema, so new object types can be added without changing the base protocol.

The mapping of EPP to an object MUST be written in a separate document that covers each command and response for that object. An appendix of RFC 5730 gives a suggested outline for such a mapping. The domain name mapping is RFC 5731.

Servers can also add an <extension> element to commands and responses, typically by agreement between client and server for unique operational needs.
sections.plainLanguage: The base protocol is a plain form with blank boxes. Other documents say what to write in the boxes for domains or other things, so the form never has to change.

sections.title: The Commands in Detail
sections.content:
A <login> MUST come before any other command. It carries a client identifier (<clID>), a case-sensitive plain text password (<pw>), an optional new password (<newPW>), the protocol version and language (which MUST exactly match the greeting) and the object URIs to be used. A <login> inside an existing session MUST be rejected. <logout> ends the session and is answered with code 1500.

Queries are read-only. <check> tells whether objects can be provisioned (an avail attribute of 1/true or 0/false), but it is only a hint because policy is up to the server. <info> returns details and the Repository Object IDentifier (ROID). <poll> retrieves queued service messages: op="req" fetches the first and op="ack" with a msgID acknowledges it so it is dequeued.

Transforms change things. <create>, <delete>, <renew> and <update> do what their names say. <transfer> moves sponsorship, using an op of request, cancel, approve, reject or query. Objects eligible for transfer MUST have authorization information that MUST be provided to complete a transfer, and a server MAY auto-approve or auto-reject requests the sponsoring client ignores.

Service messages cover things done outside a client's own request, such as deletion upon expiration, automatic renewal and transfer coordination. They never replace the normal response.
sections.plainLanguage: You log in, ask questions like "is this name free?", then make changes like adding, renewing or moving a name. If the registry leaves you a note, you read it and tick it off so the next one shows up.

sections.title: Result Codes
sections.content:
Result codes follow the reply-code approach of RFC 5321 but use four decimal digits. The first digit says whether the command worked: 1yzz is a positive completion and 2yzz a negative one where the action did not occur. The second digit gives one of six categories: protocol syntax (x0zz), implementation-specific rules (x1zz), security (x2zz), data management (x3zz), server system (x4zz) and connection management (x5zz).

Every response MUST carry a code and a description. Translations are allowed, but the code values MUST NOT change.
sections.plainLanguage: Each answer starts with a number. The first digit says yes or no, and the next digits say what kind of problem it was, like a doctor's chart code.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
EPP provides only simple client authentication, a variant of the PLAIN SASL mechanism with the identifier and password in separate XML elements. A passive attack is sufficient to recover client identifiers and passwords, so EPP instances MUST be protected by a transport that provides integrity, confidentiality and mutual, strong client-server authentication.

Servers MAY close a connection after repeated failed <login> attempts. Idempotency and transaction identifiers give some protection against replay, but a replayed <create> that follows a <delete> might succeed without further facilities to detect it. Offline-processing notices sent outside EPP's transport also need their own protection.
sections.plainLanguage: EPP's own password check is weak, like a note on a postcard. So it must always travel inside a locked, trusted tunnel built by another layer.

items.label: Action pending
items.desc: Command processed, but offline activity is needed before the action completes.

items.label: No messages
items.desc: Answer to a poll request when the queue is empty.

items.label: Ack to dequeue
items.desc: A message was retrieved from the queue.

items.label: Command use error
items.desc: Right syntax, wrong sequence or context.

items.label: Object exists
items.desc: Create attempted for an object that already exists.

items.label: Object does not exist
items.desc: Query or transform of a missing object.
